concepts.title: Computation Graph
concepts.one_liner: A computation graph is a visualization of a neural network as a sequence of modular blocks or layers chained together.
concepts.content:
A key idea of neural nets is to decompose computation into a series of layers. These layers are treated as modular blocks that can be chained together into a computation graph. For example, a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) can be represented as a sequence of layers in such a graph.

(see figure: In this chapter we will visualize neural nets as a sequence of layers, which we call a computation graph.)
concepts.motivation_md: Representing complex functions as computation graphs allows for modular design and provides a structured way to apply the chain rule for gradient calculations.
concepts.recap_md: - Decomposes complex computations into modular, chained blocks called layers.

concepts.title: Forward Pass
concepts.one_liner: The forward pass is the operation where a layer takes inputs and transforms them into outputs.
concepts.content:
Each layer in a neural network takes in some inputs and transforms them into some outputs; this is called the $\texttt{forward}$ pass through the layer. If the layer has parameters $\theta$, these are considered an input to a parameter-free transformation:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}&= f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}},\theta) \end{aligned}$$

Graphically, the forward operation of a layer is depicted as a block receiving inputs and producing an output.

(see figure: Forward operation of a neural net layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: The forward pass is the fundamental process by which a model generates a prediction or output from a given input.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps input $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and parameters $\theta$ to an output $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$.

concepts.title: Reuse of Computation in Backpropagation

position.section_title: The Trick of Backpropagation: Reuse of Computation

concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation optimizes efficiency by calculating shared terms in the chain rule once and reusing them across multiple parameter gradients.
concepts.content:
The trick of backpropagation lies in the reuse of computation. Consider a computation graph that is a chain of functions $f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots f_2 \circ f_1$, each parameterized by $\theta_l$. To optimize these parameters with respect to a loss function $\mathcal{L}$ (outputting scalar $J$), we need the gradients $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_l}$.

(see figure: Basic sequential computation graph.)
(see figure: Computation graph as a tree.)

Using the chain rule, the gradients for $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_1} &= \left( \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_L} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_3}{\partial \mathbf{x}_2} \right) \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_2}{\partial \mathbf{x}_1} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_1}{\partial \theta_1} \\ \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_2} &= \left( \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_L} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_3}{\partial \mathbf{x}_2} \right) \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_2}{\partial \theta_2} \end{aligned}$$

Most terms in these equations are shared. Rather than evaluating each gradient independently, backpropagation calculates the shared product once and reuses it for all preceding layers. This strategy is an application of dynamic programming.
concepts.motivation_md: Calculating gradients independently for every parameter would be computationally prohibitive. Reusing intermediate results makes training deep networks feasible.
concepts.recap_md: - Identifies shared terms in the chain rule to avoid redundant calculations.

key_passage.text: This is the whole trick of backpropagation: rather than computing each layer's gradients independently, observe that they share many of the same terms, so we might as well calculate each shared term once and reuse them.

motivation.text: Our goal is to update all the values highlighted in blue: θ₁, θ₂, and so forth. To do so we need to compute the gradients ∂J/∂θ₁, ∂J/∂θ₂, etc.

concepts.title: Backward Operation
concepts.one_liner: The backward operation iteratively computes gradients of the loss with respect to parameters and inputs by passing error signals backward through the network.
concepts.content:
The `backward` function is a general algorithm for reusing shared computation to update parameters. It relies on two key arrays of partial derivatives: $\mathbf{g}_l \triangleq \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_l}$ (the gradient of the cost with respect to the layer output) and $\mathbf{L} \triangleq \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \theta]}$ (the local gradient of the layer).

(see figure: A generic layer in the computation graph. The braces represent the part of the computation graph we need to consider in order to evaluate $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$, $\mathbf{L}$, and $\mathbf{g}in$.)

The gradient needed to update $\theta$ is calculated as:
$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\theta}$$

While $\mathbf{L}$ is computed locally using the derivative of the layer's function $f'$, $\mathbf{g}$ is computed iteratively using a recurrence relation:
$$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}$$

This recurrence sends error signals backward from the last layer to the first. The full `backward` operation for a generic layer takes three inputs ($\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \theta, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$) and produces two outputs ($\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta}$).
concepts.motivation_md: To minimize loss, we must know how changing each parameter affects the final error. The backward operation provides a systematic, efficient way to calculate these sensitivities for every layer.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a recurrence relation to propagate gradients $\mathbf{g}$ backward through the graph.

key_passage.text: This recurrence is essence of backprop: it sends error signals (gradients) backward through the network, starting at the last layer and iteratively applying to compute g for each previous layer.

question.text: The remaining question is clear: how do we get g_l and L^θ_l for each layer l?

motivation.text: Computing g is a bit trickier; it requires evaluating the chain rule, and depends on all the layers between x_out and J. However, this can be computed iteratively: once we know g_l, computing g_{l-1} is just one more matrix multiply!

concepts.title: Backpropagation Algorithm

position.section_title: The Full Algorithm: Forward, Then Backward

concepts.one_liner: The backpropagation algorithm computes gradients by performing a forward pass to evaluate activations and a backward pass to iteratively calculate gradients layer by layer.
concepts.content:
The full backpropagation algorithm consists of two main stages. First, a forward pass is computed through the entire network, starting with input data $\mathbf{x}_0$ and evaluating layer by layer to produce the sequence of activations $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$.

(see figure: Forward pass.)

Next, a backward pass is performed. This involves iteratively evaluating the gradients $\mathbf{g}$ to obtain the sequence $\mathbf{g}_L, \mathbf{g}_{L-1}, \ldots$, as well as the parameter gradients for each layer. The gradient update for parameters $\theta_l$ can be computed once the local Jacobian $\mathbf{L}_l$ and the incoming gradient $\mathbf{g}_l$ are available.



The algorithm ensures that operations are ordered so that the necessary arrays are ready when updating each layer.
concepts.motivation_md: To train a neural network using gradient descent, we need the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter. Backpropagation provides an efficient way to compute these gradients by reusing intermediate results from a forward pass and propagating errors backward through the chain rule.
concepts.recap_md: - Perform a forward pass to store activations for every layer.

Next, we compute a backward pass, iteratively evaluating the $\mathbf{g}$'s and obtaining the sequence $\mathbf{g}_L, \mathbf{g}_{L-1}, \ldots$, as well as the parameter gradients for each layer.

concepts.title: Backpropagation Over Data Batches
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation in batch mode computes the gradient for a whole dataset by averaging the gradients calculated for each individual datapoint.
concepts.motivation_md: In practice, neural networks are trained on large datasets. Computing gradients for the entire dataset at once is computationally efficient and provides a more stable estimate of the true gradient than using a single point.
concepts.recap_md: - The gradient of the average loss is the average of the gradients of individual losses.

key_passage.text: The gradient of a sum of terms is the sum of the gradients of each term. Therefore, to compute a gradient update for an algorithm like stochastic gradient descent, we apply backpropagation in batch mode, that is, we run it over each datapoint in our batch (which can be done in parallel) and then average the results.

motivation.text: As you may recall from previous sections, the total cost function we wish to minimize will typically be the average of the losses over all the datapoints in a training set. However, once we know how to compute the gradient for a single datapoint, we can easily compute the gradient for the whole dataset.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Linear Layer
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation for a linear layer involves matrix multiplications where the gradient with respect to inputs uses the weight matrix and the parameter gradient is an outer product.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear layers are the building blocks of MLPs. Deriving efficient matrix-based backward passes allows us to use optimized linear algebra libraries for training, avoiding the computational cost of explicit Jacobian matrices.
concepts.recap_md: - The input gradient is the output gradient multiplied by the weight matrix: $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{W}$.

key_passage.text:
The definition of a linear layer, in forward direction, is as follows: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}
\end{aligned}$$ Next we need the gradients of this function, with respect to its inputs and parameters.

motivation.text: `Forward` and `backward` for a linear layer are also very easy to write in code, using any library that provides matrix multiplication (`matmul`) as a primitive. Notice that all these operations are simple expressions, mainly involving matrix multiplies.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Pointwise Nonlinearity
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation for pointwise nonlinearities involves an element-wise multiplication of the incoming gradient with the derivative of the activation function.
concepts.content:
Pointwise nonlinearities have simple backward functions. For a scalar nonlinearity $h$ with derivative $h^{\prime}$, the layer function is $f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) = [h(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}$. The local Jacobian $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}$ is a diagonal matrix $\mathbf{H}^\prime$ containing the derivatives of the activations. The backward operation is:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{H}^\prime
\end{aligned}$$

This can be simplified to an element-wise product:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}[i] = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[i]h^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[i]) \quad \forall i 
\end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)

(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: Nonlinearities are essential for neural networks to learn complex patterns. Because they are applied element-wise, their gradients are sparse (diagonal), allowing for very efficient computation without full matrix multiplication.
concepts.recap_md: - The backward pass for a pointwise layer is an element-wise multiplication by the derivative of the activation function.

key_passage.text: Define a pointwise layer using h as f(x_in) = [h(x_in[0]), ..., h(x_in[N-1])]^T. Then we have g_in = g_out H', which can be simplified as g_in[i] = g_out[i]h'(x_in[i]) for all i.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for Loss Layers
concepts.one_liner: The backward pass for a loss layer, such as $L_2$ loss, computes the initial gradient signal as the error between predictions and ground truth.
concepts.content:
The loss layer is the final layer in an MLP. For an $L_2$ loss function $\left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2$, where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the prediction and $\mathbf{y}$ is the ground truth, the gradient with respect to the input $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} &= \frac{\partial \left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{y}}} = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})
\end{aligned}$$

Since the output of the loss layer is the cost $J$ itself, $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial J} = 1$. Thus, the backward signal $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ is simply $2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})$, which is a row vector of per-dimension errors between the prediction and the target.

(see figure: Matrix multiply for `backward` of an $L_2$ loss layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: The loss layer provides the starting point for the backward pass. It quantifies the error, which is then propagated back through the network to inform how parameters should be adjusted.
concepts.recap_md: - For $L_2$ loss, the initial backward gradient is the vector of differences $2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})$.

key_passage.text: So, the backward signal sent by the $L_2$ loss layer is a row vector of per-dimension errors between the prediction and the target.

motivation.text: The last layer we need to define for a complete MLP is the loss layer. This layer has no parameters so we only need to derive the backward equation for this layer.

concepts.title: Backpropagation through an MLP
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation through an MLP involves a forward pass to compute activations and a backward pass where linear layers use transposed weights and nonlinearities act as gates.
concepts.content:
In a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), the forward pass computes activations layer by layer.

(see figure: Forward pass through an MLP.)

For the backward pass, if we treat gradients as column vectors, the operation for a linear layer becomes $\mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{W}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$. This shows that the backward pass for a linear layer is the same operation as the forward pass, but using the transposed weight matrix.

(see figure: Backward pass through an MLP.)

In contrast, a `relu` layer in the backward pass acts as a gating matrix, masking out gradients where the forward activation was negative. Notably, all backward operations in the chain are matrix multiplications. Parameter gradients are computed at each step as an outer product between the layer's input activations $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and the incoming gradients $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the full MLP backpropagation reveals that the entire training process is composed of standard linear algebra operations, making it highly efficient to implement on modern hardware.
concepts.recap_md: - The backward pass through a linear layer is equivalent to a forward pass using transposed weights.

key_passage.text: This reveals an interesting connection between `forward` and `backward` for linear layers: `backward` for a linear layer is the same operation as `forward`, just with the weights transposed!

concepts.title: Backpropagation as a Neural Network
concepts.one_liner: The full backpropagation algorithm can be viewed as a single large neural network where the forward pass parameterizes the backward pass.
concepts.content:
The backward pass through a neural network can be implemented as another neural network, specifically a linear network where parameters are determined by the weights and activations of the original forward network. Consequently, the entire backpropagation process—forward pass followed by backward pass—is itself one large computation graph or neural network.

(see figure: The computation graph for backpropagation through a three-layer MLP. It's just another neural net! Solid lines are involved in computing data/activation gradients and dotted lines are involved in...)

This structure is an example of a **hypernetwork**, where one network (the forward pass) outputs values that parameterize another (the backward pass). An interesting property is that the backward network consists entirely of linear layers. This is because the chain rule involves products of Jacobian matrices, which represent locally linear approximations of the loss surface.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing backpropagation as a neural network helps unify the concepts of inference and training into a single framework of computation graphs, which is the basis for modern deep learning libraries.
concepts.recap_md: - Backpropagation is a hypernetwork where the forward pass provides parameters for the backward pass.

key_passage.text: the backward pass through an neural network can itself be implemented as another neural network, which is in fact a linear network with parameters determined by the weight matrices of the original network as well as by the activations in the original network. Therefore, the full backward pass is a neural network! Since the forward pass is also a neural network (the original network), the full backpropagation algorithm---a forward pass followed by a backward pass---can be viewed as just one big neural network.

motivation.text: The parameter gradients can be computed from this network via one additional matrix multiply (matmul) for each layer of the backward network.

This structure is an example of a **hypernetwork**, where one network (the forward pass) outputs values that parameterize another (the backward pass). An interesting property is that the backward network consists entirely of linear layers. This is because the chain rule involves products of Jacobian matrices, which represent locally linear approximations of the loss surface.

concepts.title: Backpropagation through DAGs

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation can be extended to Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) by using merge and branch operators to handle nodes with multiple inputs and outputs.
concepts.content: While standard backpropagation handles chain-like graphs, it can also be applied to Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) where nodes have multiple inputs and outputs. For example, a linear layer can be viewed as a DAG node with inputs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and $\theta$. Neural networks can even include cycles, which are trained using variants like backpropagation through time. To handle general DAGs, we introduce two special modules: `merge` and `branch`. (see figure: The `merge` and `branch` layers.) These operators are defined as variable concatenation and copying: $$\begin{aligned} \texttt{merge}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b) &\triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b] \\ \texttt{branch}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) &\triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}] \end{aligned}$$ The `merge` operator splits the incoming gradient vector, while the `branch` operator sums the gradients from multiple downstream paths: $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a + \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b$. These layers have no parameters, and their behavior is summarized in the following diagrams. (see figure: Merge and branch layers `forward` and `backward`.) With these layers, any DAG computation graph can be constructed.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard backpropagation is designed for sequential chains, but modern neural architectures often involve complex branching and merging of data. Generalizing backprop to DAGs allows for the training of these sophisticated models.
concepts.recap_md: - Backpropagation extends to DAGs by incorporating merge (concatenation) and branch (copying) operators.

key_passage.text: In a DAG, nodes can have multiple inputs and multiple outputs. We define them mathematically as variable concatenation and copying, respectively: merge takes two inputs and concatenates them, and branch sends copies of the same output to multiple downstream nodes.

motivation.text: To work with general DAGs, it helps to introduce two new special modules, which act to construct the topology of the graph. With merge and branch, we can construct any DAG computation graph by simply inserting these layers wherever we want a layer to have multiple inputs or multiple outputs.

concepts.title: Merge Operator

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

concepts.one_liner: The merge operator constructs the topology of a computation graph by concatenating multiple input variables into a single multidimensional output variable.
concepts.content: The merge operator is a special module used to construct the topology of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). (see figure: The `merge` and `branch` layers.) Mathematically, merge is defined as variable concatenation: $\texttt{merge}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b) \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b] \triangleq \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$. This results in a new multidimensional variable. The backward pass is straightforward; to compute the gradient $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^a$ with respect to the first input, we pick out the corresponding part of the output gradient: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^{a} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\Big[\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}, \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{b}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}\Big]^\mathsf{T} \\ &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[1, 0]^\mathsf{T} \end{aligned}$$ Thus, $\texttt{merge}$ provides an explicit way of constructing multidimensional variables for backpropagation.
concepts.motivation_md: To handle nodes with multiple inputs in a computation graph, we need a formal way to combine variables such that gradients can be correctly routed back to each specific input.
concepts.recap_md: - The merge operator concatenates multiple input variables into a single multidimensional output.

concepts.title: Branch Operator

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

concepts.one_liner: The branch operator sends copies of a single input to multiple downstream nodes, causing gradients to sum during the backward pass of backpropagation.
concepts.content: The branch operator is a special module used to construct the topology of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). (see figure: The `merge` and `branch` layers.) Mathematically, branching is defined as copying an input: $\texttt{branch}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}] \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^b]$. In this operation, copies of the same output are sent to multiple downstream nodes. Consequently, multiple gradients return to the branch module from different paths. The backward pass gradient $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ is the sum of these downstream gradients: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b] \frac{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}]}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}} \\ &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b][1, 1]^\mathsf{T} \\ &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a + \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: In complex networks, a single variable might influence multiple downstream operations; the branch operator ensures that the total influence is captured by summing gradients from all paths.
concepts.recap_md: - The branch operator sends copies of a single input variable to multiple downstream nodes.

concepts.title: Parameter Sharing
concepts.one_liner: Parameter sharing involves using a single parameter as input to multiple layers, which results in the summation of their gradients during the backpropagation process.
concepts.content: Parameter sharing occurs when a single parameter is sent as an input to multiple different layers. This can be modeled as a branching operation in a computation graph. (see figure: Parameter sharing is equivalent to branching a parameter in the computation graph.) Because it functions as a branch, the gradients for shared parameters summate. If a set of variables $\{\theta^i\}^N_{i=1}$ are all copies of one free parameter $\theta$, then the gradient is calculated as: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta^i} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Sharing parameters reduces the number of free variables in a model and allows the system to learn features that are invariant across different parts of the input or different layers.
concepts.recap_md: - Parameter sharing is equivalent to a branching operation in a computation graph.

key_passage.text: Parameter sharing consists of a single parameter being sent as input to multiple different layers.

motivation.text: Then, from the previous section, it is clear that gradients summate for shared parameters.
